subcategory: Loess Hills bluff prairie specialist grass

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained loess or sandy-loam soil in fall so the seed overwinters outdoors, since the sharp callus on each floret needs a period of cold, damp stratification plus freeze-thaw cycling to break dormancy before spring growth begins.

directions: This cool-season bunchgrass is one of the classic western Great Plains species that reaches its easternmost outposts on the steep, west-facing loess bluffs above the Missouri River, growing alongside yucca and prickly pear on thin, droughty soil that few other grasses tolerate. The common name comes from the long, sharply pointed, corkscrew-twisted awn attached to each seed, which drills itself into soil cracks (and occasionally into grazing animals) as changing humidity twists and untwists it. Plant it on an open, unmulched slope with excellent drainage and resist the urge to water or fertilize once established, since rich or wet soil causes the clumps to flop and rot. Once mature, the fine blue-green foliage and nodding, silvery seed heads add movement and texture to a dry prairie planting from late spring through fall.

planting.note: Direct sow on the surface of lean, gravelly or sandy loess soil in fall or very early spring, pressing seed in lightly without burying it, since this prairie composite germinates best with light exposure and cool, fluctuating temperatures.

directions: Hairy golden aster forms low, silvery-gray mounds of densely hairy foliage that hold their color all season, a trait that helps the plant reflect intense sun and shed moisture on the steep, exposed loess slopes where it grows best. It flowers later than most other bluff-prairie composites, opening bright golden-yellow daisy heads from midsummer into the first hard frosts, when it becomes one of the last significant nectar sources for migrating butterflies and native bees on the bluff prairie. It spreads slowly from a woody base rather than running aggressively, making it a well-behaved choice for the front of a dry gravel or rock garden border. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining soil, and skip supplemental watering except during extended drought in the first year.

subcategory: Loess Hills bluff prairie specialist legume

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall into dry, well-drained loess or limy clay-loam, since this deep-rooted legume forms a taproot almost immediately and resents the disturbance of later transplanting.

directions: Platte milkvetch is a compact, early-blooming prairie legume of dry bluff and hillside prairies along the Missouri and Platte River drainages, sending up dense, rounded clusters of cream to pale violet pea-like flowers in April and May before most other bluff-prairie forbs have started. Like other wild legumes of the loess bluffs, it fixes its own nitrogen and thrives in the kind of thin, infertile, fast-draining soil that defeats richer-ground perennials. The flowers give way to inflated, bladdery seed pods, a reliable identification feature that distinguishes this species from the larger-podded ground plum milkvetch often found on the same slopes. Once its taproot is established it needs no irrigation or fertilizer and persists for many years on an undisturbed, sunny, well-drained site.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date into dry, open or disturbed loess soil in full sun, since this deep-taprooted native germinates readily from fresh seed and quickly outcompetes shallow-rooted annuals once its root system is established.

directions: Wild four-o'clock is a sprawling, bushy prairie native with heart-shaped leaves and small, bright magenta-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and through the night, closing again by mid-morning the next day. On the Loess Hills bluffs it thrives in the same thin, loose, dry soil disturbed by slumping and erosion that keeps the steep west-facing slopes open, and its thick, carrot-like taproot lets it shrug off drought that would kill shallower-rooted companions. The evening flowers attract sphinx moths and other dusk-flying pollinators that are active after most daytime prairie flowers have closed. It self-sows readily and can be allowed to naturalize along a dry, sunny slope or gravel bank where little else will grow.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, rocky or sandy loess soil and leave undisturbed, since this long-lived species develops a deep, woody taproot almost immediately and seedlings rarely survive being dug or transplanted.

directions: Narrowleaf puccoon is one of the earliest bluff-prairie wildflowers to bloom, opening fragrant, bright lemon-yellow trumpet flowers with distinctly fringed, crimped petal edges in April and May on short stems barely above the still-brown winter grass. After the showy spring flowers fade, the plant produces a second, inconspicuous crop of small self-pollinating flowers later in the season that never fully open but still set seed, a backup strategy common in dry, unpredictable habitats. Its thick taproot reaches deep into the loess to find moisture far below the parched surface, letting it persist through the driest bluff-prairie summers without irrigation. Because the root resents disturbance, it should be seeded directly where it is to grow rather than started in containers for later transplanting.

subcategory: Loess Hills bluff prairie native thistle

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, well-drained loess prairie soil in full sun, giving plants plenty of room since established colonies spread gradually outward from creeping roots rather than staying as a single clump.

directions: Flodman's thistle is a true native prairie wildflower, easily mistaken at a glance for an unwanted weedy thistle but entirely different in behavior: it spreads slowly and modestly from shallow rhizomes to form small, stable colonies rather than aggressively overtaking disturbed ground. Its woolly, deeply lobed gray-green leaves and pink to lavender flower heads appear from mid to late summer on dry, sunny loess bluffs, providing an important nectar source for native bumblebees and swallowtail butterflies at a season when fewer prairie flowers are in bloom. Because it is frequently confused with introduced noxious thistles, it benefits from being planted in a labeled native bed or clearly bordered prairie planting rather than a casual wildflower mix. It needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established and tolerates the thin, droughty soil of an open bluff prairie without difficulty.
